D006_l001.question:
A 22-year-old single female working part-time as a barista presented with a 15-month history of psychiatric symptoms characterized by a combination of psychotic and mood disturbances. Over the past 11 months, she exhibited persistent manic features, including marked mood lability with shifts between euphoria and irritability, psychomotor agitation, inflated self-appraisal of abilities, significantly reduced need for sleep, and pressured speech. These mood-related symptoms have been accompanied by functional impairment affecting work and social domains.

Concurrent with the onset of mood symptoms, she developed psychotic symptoms over the past 10 months, including complex persecutory delusions involving beliefs of being surveilled by external agencies and visual hallucinations in which she consistently perceives non-existent figures. These hallucinations occur across settings and often contribute to increased distress and withdrawal. Avolition has progressively emerged, manifesting as diminished motivation for daily activities and personal hygiene.

Notably, delusions and visual hallucinations have persisted for over two weeks in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, fulfilling criteria for an extended psychotic episode outside the context of mania. The patient’s presentation reflects an illness course in which manic and psychotic features have largely overlapped, with mood elevation dominating the majority of the active phase.
D006_l001.options:
A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)

D006_l002.question:

Notably, there is a documented two-week period during which delusions and hallucinations persisted in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, meeting criteria for psychotic features independent of a major mood episode. Avolition has been consistently observed, contributing to deterioration in occupational performance and personal hygiene. The manic and psychotic features have co-occurred throughout much of the illness course, resulting in significant functional decline. There is no indication that recent life events temporally coincide with symptom onset; prior changes in marital or occupational status preceded symptom emergence by several years. The clinical course is consistent with a primary psychotic disorder with prominent, sustained mood disturbance.

A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    B. Schizophrenia
